newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says fully recovered, sees NATO compromise.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says fully recovered, sees NATO compromise.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, looking thin but lively on his first public appearance for nearly two months, said on Sunday he expected to strike a deal on NATO expansion plans at next month's summit with Bill Clinton.

Yeltsin, who met U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Friday, said after a wreath-laying ceremony for Russia's war dead that Moscow would stall the inclusion of its former east European allies into the western alliance as long as possible.
He told reporters he hoped to reach a compromise when he met the U.S. president in Helsinki on March 20 and 21.

"We are firm in our position. We are opposed to NATO enlargement. Our task now is to stall it as long as possible and not allow the renewal of confrontation," Yeltsin said after the short ceremony marking Russia's Defenders of the Fatherland Day.

"We have agreed to look for a compromise and I think we will find this compromise at the summit we are holding with President Clinton on March 20-21," he said at the memorial to the Unknown Soldier outside the Kremlin Wall.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov will hold talks in Brussels on Sunday with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana. It is the latest in an intensive round of diplomatic negotiations surrounding the alliance's expansion plans, which Moscow sees as a threat to security and a domestic political embarrassment.
Yeltsin spent nearly 20 minutes on the ceremony and chatting with journalists in bright sunshine.
Wearing a heavy dark blue coat, he ignored the freezing temperature and removed his fur hat during the ceremony.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and other government leaders also attended.

It was the first time Yeltsin has been seen in public since he went down with pneumonia in early January. The illness which thwarted his attempt to make an early recovery from the heart bypass operation he underwent last November. He has spent little time in the Kremlin since being re-elected last July.
Yeltsin has spoken on television and been photographed briefly during meetings with visiting officials but has not met the media or public face-to-face since New Year.
Walking a little stiffly but with confidence and speaking clearly, he told reporters he had lost 26 kg (57 pounds) during his illnesses of the past few months.
"I have fully recovered now. I just have to gain some strength," he said. "My brain is working fine."

Asked about attempts by the opposition-dominated parliament to remove him on health grounds, Yeltsin showed some of his old fire, growling: "This is a purely political, communist campaign. But they should know I am a fighter and I remain a fighter. They shouldn't attack me too hard because I can hit back."
Opposition nationalists and communists were expected to dominate parades in central Moscow on Sunday to mark the annual celebration of Russia's military might.
